variables.reason: The ledger variable 'Ra' is defined as the first-order absolute moment (mean absolute deviation) of surface-height fluctuations. The KB record pq_arithmetic_mean_roughness has canonical_quantity 'arithmetic mean roughness' with the same symbols Ra / R_a and the explicit definition 'Mean absolute deviation of surface height from its mean level'. That KB record lists si_dimension: L (length) and a supporting dimension_vector, so the candidate exponent vector with L=1 and all other base exponents 0 correctly represents Ra as a length quantity in SI. The cited record applies because it defines the exact statistical measure named Ra used in the problem and supplies the dimensionality used to validate the ledger entry.

The ledger variable 'kt' is described as peak-to-valley height. The KB record pq_peak_to_valley_height has canonical_quantity 'mean peak-to-valley roughness height' (symbols include kt) and defines it as a vertical height difference between peaks and valleys, explicitly carrying SI dimension L (length). Therefore the candidate vector with L=1 (length) and zeros elsewhere correctly represents kt. The cited record applies because it documents the same amplitude height measure and its dimensionality for roughness metrics.

The ledger variable 'k_rms' is root-mean-square roughness height. The KB record pq_rms_roughness_height explicitly defines 'root-mean-square fluctuation of surface height about its mean' with si_dimension L (length). That matches the ledger name and physical meaning, so the candidate SI exponent vector (L=1) is correct. The cited record applies because it is the canonical KB entry for k_rms and provides the dimensionality used to validate the ledger entry.

The ledger variable 'Sk' is defined as the skewness of surface-height fluctuations. The KB record pq_height_skewness defines 'surface-height skewness' as the third standardized moment and lists si_dimension: 1 (dimensionless). Since standardized moments are dimensionless by construction, the ledger vector with all zero exponents correctly represents Sk. The cited KB entry is the canonical definition for Sk in the retrieved dataset and therefore directly supports the dimensional claim.

The ledger variable 'Ku' is the kurtosis (fourth standardized moment) of surface-height fluctuations. The KB record pq_height_kurtosis defines this canonical quantity and lists si_dimension: 1 (dimensionless). Therefore the candidate vector with all base exponents zero correctly represents Ku. The cited KB record applies because it documents the exact standardized moment used in the problem and provides its dimensionality.

The ledger variable 'ES' is given as effective streamwise slope (mean absolute surface slope). The KB record pq_effective_surface_slope defines mean absolute gradient of surface height in a horizontal direction, notes that a surface-height derivative is length/length and thus dimensionless (si_dimension: 1). Therefore the ledger vector with all zeros correctly captures ES as dimensionless. The cited record applies because it is the KB entry for the effective surface slope with the same meaning and dimensional statement.

The ledger variable 'Po' is surface porosity (fractional open area). The KB record pq_porosity defines porosity as a dimensionless fraction (si_dimension: 1). Hence the candidate all-zero exponent vector correctly represents Po as dimensionless. The cited KB entry applies because it documents the same porosity measure and its dimensional status used in the problem.

candidate_ledger.output_variable_reasoning: ks/Ra is the normalized equivalent sand-grain roughness (ratio of a length ks to the first-order absolute moment Ra). Since ks and Ra both have dimensions of length, the ratio ks/Ra is dimensionless. The seven provided input parameters include three length-like measures (Ra, kt, k_rms) and four purely statistical or geometric, dimensionless descriptors (Sk, Ku, ES, Po). By Buckingham Pi, the target dimensionless group ks/Ra can only depend on dimensionless combinations of the inputs; length inputs must appear in nondimensional ratios (e.g., kt/Ra, k_rms/Ra) while the purely dimensionless inputs (Sk, Ku, ES, Po) may appear directly. Therefore the governing relation can be written in nondimensional form ks/Ra = F(kt/Ra, k_rms/Ra, Sk, Ku, ES, Po). This reasoning assumes classical SI base dimensions and that all supplied statistical descriptors (Sk, Ku, ES, Po) are dimensionless by construction.

variables.physical_definition: First-order absolute moment of surface height fluctuations (mean absolute deviation of height from the mean).
Peak-to-valley height of the rough surface (maximum vertical distance between highest peak and deepest valley).
Root-mean-square height of surface roughness (standard deviation of height deviations).
Skewness of roughness height fluctuations (third standardized moment, dimensionless).
Kurtosis of roughness height fluctuations (fourth standardized moment, dimensionless).
Effective streamwise slope of the roughness (mean local slope in the flow direction, dimensionless).
Surface porosity (fractional open area of the surface, dimensionless).

Problem:
Perform dimensional analysis for sand-grain roughness parameterization to derive the dimensionless relationship governing the normalized equivalent sand-grain roughness (denoted as ks/Ra).
This analysis uses ONLY the following 7 physical quantities as input parameters:
the first-order absolute moment of height fluctuations, Ra;
the peak-to-valley height, kt;
the root-mean-square height, k_rms;
the skewness of roughness height fluctuations, Sk;
the kurtosis of roughness height fluctuations, Ku;
the effective streamwise slope of the roughness, ES;
the surface porosity, Po.

variables.physical_definition: First-order absolute moment of surface height fluctuations (mean absolute deviation of height from the mean).
Peak-to-valley height of the rough surface (maximum vertical distance between highest peak and deepest valley).
Root-mean-square height of surface roughness (standard deviation of height deviations).
Skewness of roughness height fluctuations (third standardized moment, dimensionless).
Kurtosis of roughness height fluctuations (fourth standardized moment, dimensionless).
Effective streamwise slope of the roughness (mean local slope in the flow direction, dimensionless).
Surface porosity (fractional open area of the surface, dimensionless).
